item.title: Nanostructuring Semiconductor Surfaces Using Self-Assembled Metal Nanoparticles for Optoelectronic Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.14292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semiconductor nanostructures are key light-management elements because their geometry can strengthen light-matter interaction, suppress reflection, and enhance optical coupling. Yet their adoption across material platforms is constrained by lithography, multistep pattern transfer, persistent masks, and material-specific etching. Here, we introduce a lithography-free two-step strategy in which thermally evaporated self-assembled Ga nanoparticles act as self-consuming masks during Ar inductively coupled plasma reactive-ion etching. Correlated transmission electron microscopy on GaAs reveals the formation mechanism. Comparable erosion of the Ga nanoparticles and exposed substrate progressively converts Ga-capped pedestals into pure semiconductor nanocones while preserving crystalline order. Nanocone dimensions extend from tens to hundreds of nanometres, and surface coverage is tunable through Ga deposition and plasma power. The same process produces nanocones on GaP and Si and dense nanostructures on polycrystalline hybrid metal-halide perovskite without detectable PbI2 formation. During nanostructuring, the sun-weighted reflectance reaches minima of 11-15% on the monocrystalline substrates, whereas the perovskite achieves 0.5% after complete mask consumption. The approach therefore combines a self-assembled mask, its consumption, and pattern transfer in a single physical etching step, providing a simple route to light-coupling surfaces for III-V, Si, and perovskite optoelectronics.

item.title: Molecular Gas Optics Using Vibrational Population Density Refraction
item.description: arXiv:2611.13242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gas optics holds promise for development of advanced optical elements with 2-3 orders of magnitude higher damage threshold than any solid-state optics. Here, we demonstrate a new concept for refracting the laser beam using vibrationally excited molecules as gas optics instead of traditional control of thermodynamic gas temperature. The transient, vibrational population density grating is formed in a CO2 gas by interfering two mid-IR lasers to imprint spatial modulation in the linear refractive index (Delta n0 >=2x10-5) of the neutral gas via enhancement of the molecular polarizability. It is increased by pumping the asymmetric stretching mode of CO2 at optimal wavelengths to resonantly produce a highly nonequilibrium state that increases the effective vibrational mode temperature to greater than 2000 K in a room temperature gas. The measured beam steering efficiency of such a volume gas grating exceeds 90% that makes this approach a candidate for producing other large-aperture, high-throughput molecular optics elements, with expected damage thresholds 0.5-1 kJ/cm2, much-needed for future ultrahigh-power lasers.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Matteo, Sergei Tochitsky, Chan Joshi

item.title: Optically modulated field-dependent electrical response in a non-collinear antiferromagnet/ferromagnet heterostructure
item.description: arXiv:2611.13351v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The interplay among optical, electrical, and magnetic stimuli offers opportunities to control the functional response of spintronic heterostructures. Here, we investigate the field-dependent electrical response of MgO/IrMn$_3$/Py/Au under radio-frequency (RF) excitation, white-light illumination, and direct-current (DC) bias. Under a 20 MHz RF signal with a nominal power of 2 W, the measured voltage in the dark remains at several tens of nanovolts. Upon illumination with approximately 1 W of white light, a pronounced field-dependent feature emerges around 315--320 Oe, reaching 0.9--1.0 $\mu$V. The illumination-associated differential voltage is approximately 0.95 $\mu$V. A DC current of 1 mA produces a response of approximately 1 $\mu$V, while the simultaneous application of RF, DC, and optical excitation increases the voltage to approximately 1.8 $\mu$V. Magnetic characterization reveals exchange bias with a blocking temperature near 380 K, while electrical resistance measurements show a pronounced dependence on magnetic-field orientation, consistent with the anisotropic response of the heterostructure. These results demonstrate that the field-dependent electrical response can be modulated through combined optical and electrical excitation, involving magneto-optical interactions and spin-dependent transport phenomena, potentially including spin Hall-related contributions and the magnetic spin Hall effect. This work provides insights into coupled optical, electrical, and magnetic-field effects in heterostructures based on non-collinear antiferromagnets and ferromagnetic layers.
item.dc:creator: Adrielson Dias, Andr\'e Jos\'e, Jos\'e Lucas, Rodrigo Cristian, Jos\'e Holanda

item.title: Additively manufactured ceramic platforms for miniaturized optical frequency references and robust atomic sensor systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.13800v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transferring atomic quantum sensors from laboratory-scale physics packages to compact, alignment-free sensor heads suitable for field and space deployment requires a structural platform that combines mechanical, thermal, and optical functionality within a single, manufacturable component. We present such a platform based on additively manufactured technical ceramics: lithography-based ceramic manufacturing is used to fabricate monolithic micro-optical benches with application-specific mounting geometries, while high-precision active alignment and adhesive bonding realize long-term stable optical assemblies through micro-integration. As a first system-level demonstrator, we present a micro-integrated optical frequency reference based on Doppler-free spectroscopy of the rubidium D2 line, integrated within a 6 mL Al2O3 module. A laser stabilized to the reference reaches a fractional frequency instability of $3\times10^{-12}$ at 1 s. We extend the platform to a compact optically pumped magnetometer, exploiting the magnetic cleanliness and tailored thermal properties of high-purity ceramics for a 7 mL sensor head with picotesla sensitivity aimed at space-borne biomagnetometry, and to a micro-integrated optical dipole trap with active MEMS-mirror beam steering for cold-atom manipulation. Together, these demonstrators show that ceramic additive manufacturing and optical micro-integration form a versatile, robust platform for compact atomic sensor systems in field and space applications.

item.title: Bare and stretched string tyre models with distributed FrBD dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2603.02869v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a novel class of string tyre models with FrBD friction dynamics. By modelling the distributed carcass and tread deformations with string-like equations, the resulting formulation leads to a system of semilinear parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) that describe the evolution of the tyre states without explicitly distinguishing between stick and slip regimes. Rigorous stability and passivity analyses are also conducted using a Lyapunov-based approach, establishing boundedness of the distributed states and energy dissipation during rolling contact. The proposed Lyapunov function admits a clear physical interpretation as the total elastic energy stored in the tyre, enabling a direct link between mechanical energy storage and frictional dissipation due to slip losses. The steady-state and transient behaviours of the model are investigated both numerically and experimentally, revealing that the new formulation can satisfactorily reproduce nonlinear relaxation phenomena excited by step slip inputs. The resulting model provides a physically interpretable, mathematically well-posed, and computationally efficient basis for advanced vehicle dynamics simulations and control-oriented applications.
item.dc:creator: Luigi Romano

item.title: Improving the vibration isolation efficiency of chiral phononic crystals through viscoelastic damping
item.description: arXiv:2606.01272v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mechanical phononic crystals attenuate vibration transmission in a wide frequency range called the bandgap. Chiral phononic crystals have demonstrated their ability to achieve low-frequency bandgaps while maintaining a high static stiffness. However, their design is non-trivial because of the complex geometry involved. Furthermore, bandgap generation in phononic crystals relies on wave scattering rather than energy dissipation, which leads to important local vibration amplitudes. In this paper, viscoelastic inserts are introduced with two goals: improve the crystal's tunability in terms of stiffness and bandgap properties, and employ damping to reduce internal resonances. First, the fundamental effect of viscous damping in phononic crystals is investigated through analytical equivalent models, showing that moderate damping improves the vibration isolation by merging multiple bandgaps. As a real-world example, highly viscoelastic polyurethane is studied by examining the influence of its frequency-dependent storage modulus and loss factor. Three crystals with different viscoelastic inserts are manufactured and the measured force transmissibility is successfully compared to the numerical models. The results show that the storage modulus correlates strongly with vibration isolation efficiency, defining both the frequency range and the maximum force reduction, whereas a loss modulus broadens the vibration isolation frequency range without negatively affecting its efficiency when it stays below a critical threshold value.

item.title: Designing Strong and Broadband Nonreciprocal Thermal Radiation in Magnetic Topological Materials
item.description: arXiv:2606.14861v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Breaking reciprocity in thermal radiation opens opportunities for energy harvesting, sensing, and thermal management. Traditional nonreciprocal radiative semiconductor devices need external magnetic field. In this work, we predict a series of magnetic topological materials for magnetic-field-free nonreciprocal thermal radiation in the infrared regime, by combining first-principles calculations with Maxwell electrodynamics. We find strong and broadband nonreciprocity in magnetic Weyl semimetals (e.g., Co$_3$Sn$_2$S$_2$), outperforming the conventional semiconductor such as InAs. Furthermore, we propose universal material design recipes: strong nonreciprocity requires a large anomalous Hall response relative to the optical loss, whereas the broadband response favors large optical loss and small dielectric dispersion. Our work establishes a predictive materials-discovery framework and quantitative design rules for next-generation magnet-free nonreciprocal thermal devices.
item.dc:creator: Yiyang Jiang, Yufei Zhao, Linxiao Zhu, Binghai Yan

item.title: High Precision Fundamental Physics Experiments at JLab with Spin-transparent Storage Rings of Low-energy Polarized Electron Beams
item.description: arXiv:2608.08551v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A breakthrough in fundamental physics experiments measuring particle spin precession may happen if spin-transparent storage rings become adopted tools for such experiments. We present a new design of highly specialized table-sized storage rings, which use low-energy polarized electron beams and Mott polarimetry. Based on the spin transparency ansatz, the spin precession stemming from the magnetic dipole moment is canceled at any beam energy after an electron's turn along the periodic orbit in the ring. Meanwhile, a spin precession induced by the fundamental physics of interest, e.g., the electron's permanent electric dipole moment (EDM) and/or ultralight-dark-matter-mediated forces such as axions, will accumulate. However, capitalizing on such types of rings is not only desirable for measurements of EDMs and axion searches relevant to $CP$ violation and matter-antimatter asymmetry in the Universe, but may also find very promising applications in quantum computing.
